passage:
"Football again?" Kishore said. "Raghav, you're on my side."
"Okay," Raghav said, though he'd wanted to play carrom.
Later the ball smashed the staffroom window. "Who kicked it?" the PT sir asked.
Kishore went pale. Raghav stepped forward. "Me, sir."
After school Kishore caught up with him. "Why did you say that? It was my kick."
"You looked scared. I didn't want a fight."
"You hate football, don't you?"
Raghav shrugged. "Everyone was happy."
"I'd still be your friend if you said no, you know. Tomorrow, carrom?"
Raghav looked up. "Really?"
"Really. And I'm telling sir it was me."

qa.q: What had Raghav wanted to play instead?
qa.a: He'd wanted to play carrom.

qa.q: Why did Raghav take the blame for the broken window?
qa.a: He felt Kishore was scared and wanted to avoid a fight; keeping everyone happy felt safer to him.

qa.q: What turning point came when Kishore caught up after school?
qa.a: Kishore said they would still be friends if Raghav said no and offered carrom, showing that refusing would not end the friendship.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel when Raghav took the blame for Kishore's kick?
qa.a: Kishore seems uncomfortable and guilty, which is why Kishore decides to tell sir the truth.

grounding: A boy agrees to games he dislikes and takes blame to avoid conflict, and his friend shows him that saying no won't break their friendship.

passage:
Last year I was the one who always said, "I don't mind." If Gargi wanted to play house, I played house, even though I wanted to draw. When our group fought over who spilled ink on the class chart, I said it was me, just so the shouting would stop. It wasn't me. I felt calm for about a minute, and then heavy for the whole day. One evening I told my Masi about the ink, and she said, "A friend who leaves because you said no was never really your friend." The next week, when Gargi said house again, I said, "Can we draw first?" She blinked, then said, "Okay, draw first." Nothing broke.
Hansa

qa.q: What did Hansa want to do instead of playing house?
qa.a: Hansa wanted to draw.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel after taking the blame for the ink?
qa.a: Hansa felt calm for about a minute and then heavy for the whole day.

qa.q: What choice did Hansa make the next week, and what happened?
qa.a: Hansa asked to draw first, and Gargi simply agreed, so nothing broke.

qa.q: What might Gargi have thought when Hansa finally asked to draw first?
qa.a: She was a little surprised, but happy to go along, which shows she cared more about the friendship than the game.

grounding: A child who always agreed and even took blame to keep the peace learns, with an aunt's help, that saying no does not break a friendship.

passage: In the colony park in Chennai, Minakshi always chose the game, and Gopika always said yes. Today it was hide-and-seek again, which Gopika hated: the dark corner behind the watchman's cabin made her stomach tight. She hid there anyway. Later Minakshi's ball smashed Mrs. Rao's flowerpot. Mrs. Rao came out, furious. 'Who did this?' Minakshi went pale. 'I did,' Gopika said quickly. 'Sorry, Aunty.' At home, Amma had already heard from Mrs. Rao. 'Why did you say it was you?' Gopika's eyes filled. 'Minakshi would cry. Then nobody would play.' Amma sat beside her. 'If you tell the truth, or say no to hide-and-seek, will Minakshi stop being your friend?' Gopika didn't know. That scared her most.

qa.q: Whose flowerpot did the ball smash?
qa.a: Mrs. Rao's.

qa.q: Why did Gopika say 'I did'?
qa.a: She was anxious about conflict; if Minakshi cried nobody would play, and she only feels safe when everyone is happy.

qa.q: How could Amma help Gopika after this?
qa.a: Help her practise small, kind 'no's and telling the truth, and show her that friends usually stay even when she disagrees.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel about Gopika taking the blame?
qa.a: Minakshi was probably relieved at first, but may also feel uneasy or guilty that Gopika took the blame for Minakshi's ball.

grounding: Shows a child who agrees to games she dislikes and takes the blame to avoid conflict, and a parent beginning to help her see that no won't end a friendship.

passage:
'You look tired, Gopu.'
'I played teacher-teacher with Rinku again. I'm always the student who gets scolded.'
'Do you like being the student?'
'No. I like drawing.' Gopika picked at the sofa. 'But Rinku gets upset if I say no. Then she won't talk to me.'
'For how long?'
Gopika thought. 'Last time, till lunch.'
'And then?'
'Then she wanted to sit with me.'
'So a no costs you one morning, and she still comes back.' Vidya grinned. 'Let's practise. I'm Rinku. Gopika, come play teacher-teacher!'
Gopika giggled, then took a breath. 'Not today. I want to draw. Tomorrow I'll play.'
'Hmph,' said Vidya-as-Rinku. 'Okay. Can I watch you draw?'
'Rinku wouldn't say that.'
'Try it and see.'

qa.q: What does Gopika like doing instead of playing teacher-teacher?
qa.a: Drawing.

qa.q: What is Gopika afraid will happen if she says no to Rinku?
qa.a: She is anxious that Rinku will get upset and stop talking to her.

qa.q: How did Vidya help Gopika see that saying no is safe?
qa.a: By asking what happened last time, Rinku sulked till lunch and then came back, and by letting her practise a kind no.

qa.q: Why might Rinku react differently from how Gopika fears?
qa.a: Last time Rinku only sulked till lunch and then wanted to sit with Gopika, so the friendship may be sturdier than Gopika thinks.

grounding: Shows a child who keeps agreeing to a game she dislikes to keep a friend happy, and an older person helping her practise saying no.

passage: Last year I was the peacemaker of 6B. I'm Darshan. If two people fought over the class cricket bat, I gave up my turn. If the group wanted football, which I hate, I played goalkeeper and let everything in. When our science model fell off the desk, and it was really Rahul's elbow, I said it was me so Ma'am wouldn't shout at him. I only felt calm when everyone was smiling. Then Nazia, who sits next to me, said something that stuck: 'You know you're allowed to not want things, right?' I laughed. But the next week I told the group, 'I'll skip football today. I'm going to the library.' My heart was thumping. Nobody minded. Rahul still sat with me at lunch.

qa.q: What did Darshan tell the group the next week?
qa.a: 'I'll skip football today. I'm going to the library.'

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling when saying no to football?
qa.a: Darshan felt nervous, heart thumping, afraid that saying no would cost friendships.

qa.q: What helped Darshan start saying no?
qa.a: Nazia's remark that it's allowed to not want things, and then trying one small no and seeing that nothing broke.

qa.q: How might Rahul have felt when Darshan took the blame for his elbow?
qa.a: Rahul may have felt relieved to escape a scolding, but perhaps also guilty that Darshan paid for his mistake.

grounding: Shows a child who agrees to disliked games and takes the blame to keep the peace, and learns that saying no does not end friendships.

passage:
Class note, Year 4, Friday. Written by Deepak.
Bhavna, nine, is loved by everyone. This week I saw why, and also what it costs her. At break she played "teacher" three days running, always as the scolded student, though I know she wanted to play hopscotch. On Wednesday, when a clay pot broke, she said, "It was me," though I'd seen another child knock it. She looked relieved once the fuss ended.
I spoke to her quietly after class. She said, "If everyone's happy, I feel safe." We practised a few sentences: "I want to play hopscotch today," and "I didn't break it." On Friday she tried the first one. Her friends switched games without a fuss. She came back beaming.

qa.q: What game did Bhavna want to play?
qa.a: Hopscotch.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel after taking the blame for the pot?
qa.a: She felt relieved once the fuss ended, because conflict made her feel unsafe.

qa.q: How did Deepak help Bhavna learn that saying no is safe?
qa.a: Deepak spoke with her privately and practised simple sentences to say what she wants and what is true.

qa.q: How did Bhavna's friends react when she said what she wanted?
qa.a: They switched games without any fuss, showing her the friendship was still safe.

grounding: Shows a people-pleasing child who agrees to disliked games and takes blame to avoid conflict, and a teacher helping her learn that saying no doesn't break friendship.
